{{Short description|Type of function}}
{{about|the notion in convex analysis|the notion in several complex variables|pseudoconvex domain}}
In [[convex analysis]] and the [[calculus of variations]], both branches of [[mathematics]], a '''pseudoconvex function''' is a [[function (mathematics)|function]] that behaves like a [[convex function]] with respect to finding its [[local extrema|local minima]], but need not actually be convex.  Informally, a differentiable function is pseudoconvex if it is increasing in any direction where it has a positive [[directional derivative]]. The property must hold in all of the function domain, and not only for nearby points.

==Formal definition==

Consider a [[differentiable]] function <math>f:X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math>, defined on a (nonempty) [[convex set|convex]] [[open set]] <math>X</math> of the finite-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>. This function is said to be '''pseudoconvex''' if the following property holds:<ref>{{harvnb|Mangasarian|1965}}</ref>

: for all <math>x,y \in X: \quad \nabla f(x) \cdot (y-x) \geq 0 \Rightarrow f(y) \geq f(x).</math>

Equivalently:

: for all <math>x,y \in X: \quad f(y) < f(x) \Rightarrow \nabla f(x) \cdot (y-x) < 0.</math>

Here <math>\nabla f</math> is the [[gradient]] of <math>f</math>, defined by: <math>\nabla f = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1},\dots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\right).</math>

Note that the definition may also be stated in terms of the [[directional derivative]] of <math>f</math>, in the direction given by the vector <math>v=y-x</math>. This is because, as <math>f</math> is differentiable, this directional derivative is given by:

: <math>\frac{\partial f}{\partial v}(x) = \nabla f(x) \cdot v = \nabla f(x) \cdot (y-x).</math>
==Properties==

=== Relation to other types of "convexity" ===

Every convex function is pseudoconvex, but the converse is not true. For example, the function <math>f(x) = x + x^{3}</math> is pseudoconvex but not convex. Similarly, any pseudoconvex function is [[quasiconvex function|quasiconvex]]; but the converse is not true, since the function <math>f(x) = x^{3}</math> is quasiconvex but not pseudoconvex. This can be summarized schematically as:

: convex <math>\Rightarrow</math> pseudoconvex <math>\Rightarrow</math> quasiconvex

[[File:Pseudoquasiconvex.png|thumb|alt=Functions x^3 (quasiconvex but not pseudoconvex) and x^3 + x (pseudoconvex and thus quasiconvex). None of them is convex.|Functions x^3 (quasiconvex but not pseudoconvex) and x^3 + x (pseudoconvex and thus quasiconvex). None of them is convex.]]

To see that <math>f(x) = x^{3}</math> is not pseudoconvex, consider its derivative at <math>x = 0</math>: <math>f^{\prime}(0) = 0</math>. Then, if <math>f(x) = x^{3}</math> was pseudoconvex, we should have:

: <math>f^{\prime}(0) (y-0) = 0 \geq 0 \Rightarrow f(y) \geq f(0), \quad \forall \, y \in \mathbb{R}.</math>

In particular it should be true for <math>y=-1</math>. But it is not, as: <math>f(-1) = (-1)^{3} = -1 < f(0) = 0</math>.

=== Sufficient optimality condition ===

For any differentiable function, we have the [[Fermat's theorem (stationary points)|Fermat's theorem]] necessary condition of optimality, which states that: if <math>f</math> has a local minimum at <math>x^{*}</math> in an [[open set|open]] domain, then <math>x^{*}</math> must be a [[stationary point]] of <math>f</math> (that is: <math>\nabla f(x^{*}) = 0</math>).

Pseudoconvexity is of great interest in the area of [[optimization]], because the converse is also true for any pseudoconvex function. That is:<ref>{{harvnb|Mangasarian|1965}}</ref> if <math>x^{*}</math> is a [[stationary point]] of a pseudoconvex function <math>f</math>, then <math>f</math> has a global minimum at <math>x^{*}</math>. Note also that the result guarantees a global minimum (not only local).

This last result is also true for a convex function, but it is not true for a quasiconvex function. Consider for example the quasiconvex function:

: <math>f(x)=\frac{e^{x}}{x^{2}+1} + \frac{1}{e^{x}}.</math>

This function is not pseudoconvex, but it is quasiconvex. Also, the point <math>x=0</math> is a critical point of <math>f</math>, as <math>f^{\prime}(0)=0</math>. However, <math>f</math> does not have a global minimum at <math>x=0</math> (not even a local minimum).

[[File:Quasiconvex optimality.png|thumb|alt=Example of a quasiconvex function with a critical point that is not a minimum.|Example of a quasiconvex function that is not pseudoconvex. The function has a critical point at <math>x=0</math>, but this is not a minimum.]]

Finally, note that a pseudoconvex function may not have any critical point. Take for example the pseudoconvex function: <math>f(x)=x^{3}+x</math>, whose derivative is always positive: <math>f^{\prime}(x)=3x^{2}+1>0, \, \forall \, x \in \mathbb{R}</math>.

==Examples==

An example of a function that is pseudoconvex, but not convex, is: <math>f(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+k}, \, k > 0.</math> The figure shows this function for the case where <math>k=0.2</math>. This example may be generalized to two variables as:

: <math>f(x)=\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{x^{2}+y^{2}+k}, \, k > 0.</math>

[[File:Pseudoconvex.png|thumb|alt=Pseudoconvex function that is not convex: x^2 / (x^2+0.2)|Pseudoconvex function that is not convex.]]

The previous example may be modified to obtain a function that is not convex, nor pseudoconvex, but is quasiconvex:

: <math>f(x)=\frac{|x|^{p}}{|x|^{p}+k}, \, k > 0, \, p \in (0,1).</math>

The figure shows this function for the case where <math>k=0.5, p=0.6</math>. As can be seen, this function is not convex because of the concavity, and it is not pseudoconvex because it is not differentiable at <math>x=0</math>.

[[File:Quasiconvex.png|thumb|alt=Quasiconvex function that is not convex, nor pseudoconvex: <nowiki>{{!}}x{{!}}^0.6 / ( {{!}}x{{!}}^0.6 + 0.5 )</nowiki>|Quasiconvex function that is not convex, nor pseudoconvex.]]

==Generalization to nondifferentiable functions==

The notion of pseudoconvexity can be generalized to nondifferentiable functions as follows.<ref>{{harvnb|Floudas|Pardalos|2001}}</ref> Given any function <math>f:X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math>, we can define the upper [[Dini derivative]] of <math>f</math> by:

: <math>f^{+}(x,u) = \limsup_{ h \to 0^{+} } \frac{f(x+hu) - f(x)}{h};</math>

where ''u'' is any [[unit vector]]. The function is said to be pseudoconvex if it is increasing in any direction where the upper Dini derivative is positive. More precisely, this is characterized in terms of the [[subdifferential]] <math>\partial f</math> as follows:

: For all <math>x, y \in X</math>: if <math>x^* \in \partial f(x)</math> is such that <math>\langle x^* , y - x \rangle \geq 0</math>, then <math>f(x) \leq f(z)</math>, for all <math>z \in [x,y]</math>;

where <math>[x,y]</math> denotes the line segment adjoining ''x'' and ''y''.

==Related notions==

A '''{{visible anchor|pseudoconcave function}}''' is a function whose negative is pseudoconvex. A '''{{visible anchor|pseudolinear function}}''' is a function that is both pseudoconvex and pseudoconcave.<ref>{{harvnb|Rapcsak|1991}}</ref> For example, [[linear-fractional programming|linear–fractional program]]s have pseudolinear [[objective function]]s and [[linear programming|linear–inequality constraints]]. These properties allow fractional-linear problems to be solved by a variant of the [[simplex algorithm]] (of [[George B. Dantzig]]).<ref>
Chapter five: {{cite book| last=Craven|first=B. D.|title=Fractional programming|series=Sigma Series in Applied Mathematics|volume=4|publisher=Heldermann Verlag|location=Berlin|year=1988|pages=145|isbn=3-88538-404-3 |mr=949209}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Kruk | first1=Serge|last2=Wolkowicz|first2=Henry|title=Pseudolinear programming |journal=[[SIAM Review]]|volume=41 |year=1999 |number=4 |pages=795–805 |mr=1723002 | jstor = 2653207 |doi=10.1137/S0036144598335259| bibcode=1999SIAMR..41..795K}}
</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Mathis|first1=Frank H.|last2=Mathis|first2=Lenora Jane|title=A nonlinear programming algorithm for hospital management |journal=[[SIAM Review]]|volume=37 |year=1995 |number=2 |pages=230–234|mr=1343214 | jstor = 2132826 |doi=10.1137/1037046|s2cid=120626738 }}
</ref>

Given a vector-valued function <math>\eta</math>, there is a more general notion of <math>\eta</math>-pseudoconvexity<ref name="Ansari2013">{{cite book |last1=Ansari |first1=Qamrul Hasan |last2=Lalitha |first2=C. S. |last3=Mehta |first3=Monika |title=Generalized Convexity, Nonsmooth Variational Inequalities, and Nonsmooth Optimization |date=2013 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=9781439868218 |page=107 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3qzMBQAAQBAJ&q=pseudolinearity&pg=PA107 |access-date=15 July 2019 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Mishra2008">{{cite book |last1=Mishra |first1=Shashi K. |last2=Giorgi |first2=Giorgio |title=Invexity and Optimization |date=2008 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=9783540785613 |page=39 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SDbS50KIQGIC&q=pseudolinearity&pg=PA39 |access-date=15 July 2019 |language=en}}</ref> and <math>\eta</math>-pseudolinearity; wherein classical pseudoconvexity and pseudolinearity pertain to the case when <math>\eta (x, y) = y - x</math>.
